newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sasol, Norway's Statoil to form alliance.
newsitem.headline: Sasol, Norway's Statoil to form alliance.

text.p: South African fuels and chemicals firm Sasol Ltd said on Monday it will form a technological alliance with Norway's Statoil on converting natural gas to synthetic crude oil and liquid fuels.

Sasol said in a statement that the rationale behind the alliance with state-owned Statoil, a leading explorer, producer and marketer of oil and gas in Northern Europe, is the mutually complementary technology capabilities of the two firms.

Sasol could provide technology for the conversion of gas to synthetic crude oil and liquid fuels by the Fischer-Tropsch technology, while Statoil will provide offshore and floating production technology for oil and gas.
"Statoil prefers to co-operate with Sasol rather than rely on the further development of its own Ficher-Tropsch technology," the statement said.

It said the two firms were already underway with the development of a concept for a floating Fischer-Tropsch conversion plant which could be placed on a ship or offshore production system used for gas and oil production, converting the gas to synthetic crude.

Such facilities would allow the natural gas to be utilised at the point of production, rather than being piped ashore or re-injected into the reservoir. This can also eliminate the flaring of natural gas and its associated environmental damage.
The firms also planned to market these floating gas conversion facilities on a commercial basis to other oil and gas businesses.
Sasol and Statoil will co-operate exclusively in developing the production system, and on a non-exclusive case-by-case basis, for other applications.
"It is the intention that both parties will be able to hold equity in facilities arising from the exploitation of opportunities to convert gas to oils and fuels."
Of particular interest to Sasol is the possible utilisation of Statoil's large gas reserves in Northern Europe, which is estimated in excess of 50 trillion cubic feet.
Sasol announced last month that it was holding discussions with the Qatar General Petroleum Corp with the intention of establishing a joint venture project to convert natural gas to liquid fuels.

The proposed project would be sited at Ras Laffan in Qatar and would convert some of Qatar's abundant natural gas reserves into transportation liquid fuels, such as diesel, using Sasol's commercially-proven technology, Sasol said in a statement.
In an interview with Reuters last month Sasol said that part of its strategy for growth was finding partners for its Fischer Tropsch conversion technology.
Managing director Pieter Cox said then that the first of several possible deals could be unveiled within two years, but the agreements will not involve licensing out the cutting edge technology.
